Monday, October 12, 2026 A15 OPINION # How the AI Boom Ends INSIDE VIEW By Andy Kessler I can tell you how the artificial-intelligence data-center boom will probably end, but I can't tell you when. Implementing large language models has been a brute-force approach: Big, fast and expensive GPUs from Nvidia crunch a trillion parameters using massive amounts of memory housed in liquid-cooled, gigawatt-gobbling data centers, all with brute-force pricing. It sure smells like IBM making a deal with the Be careful about extrapolating anything from today's pricing. With AI, like all new technologies, the refinement stage is looming — just as the frames gave way to cheaper minicomputers, microprocessors, web servers and now AI architectures. AI tokens have been dropping but are set to plunge faster than most anticipate. Tech growth is never a straight line. Silicon Valley's mantra for decades has been smaller, cheaper, faster, better. I asked venture capitalist Steve Jutreson to translate that into numbers. "We often see a technology shift when the new approach is 10 times better. It can be 10 times more performant or 10 times cheaper, sometimes both." He calls it the "factor of 10." And it's happening. Last week, according to OpenRouter, OpenAI and Anthropic were charging a premium for some of their models—$1 to$2 per million input tokens. Comparable Chinese open-weight models like Zai's GLM and Alibaba's Qwen charged 6 to 12 cents, around 90% less—that factor of 10 inflection point. American AI labs have gone from 70% market share last year to 30% today. All are still growing. But prices must be less可怕 than the large language models, right? Not really. Stanford researchers show that a locally run small language model "can successfully answer 88.7% of single-turn chat and reasoning queries." No question we'll always have high- and low- and low- and low- Where? Another Silicon Valley saying I've lived by: Intelligence moves out to the edge of the network. The real breakthrough will happen when robust AI models run on smartphones. It's already starting. In September, California-based PrismLl released a compressed version of the popular open-source Qwen3.8 27B AI model. The company got it down to under 6 gigabytes. That means it fits not only on PCs but also on high-end smartphones. The memory size is reduced by roughly 9 to 10 times. There's that factor of 10. Technology doesn't stand still. Qualcomm recently announced a new Snapdragon neural processing unit, or NPU, for smartphones. Using what the company calls a "miture-of-experts" model, it could run a 30 billion parameter AI model in 3 gigabytes of memory. According to the DeepMind, the large AI model on a phone has been four billion parameters on an Apple A20 Pro chip. Qualcomm provides a 7.5 times boost. Demand isn't about to let up, but prices will start plunging by factors of 10. NPUs, like Qualcomm's new Snapdragon and Google's Tensor chips in its Pixel phones, are now making the same for the latest Apple M- and A-series chips, engines that can run AI models locally on iPhones—maybe why Apple hasn't joined the AI data-center spending delirium. A Nvidia-backed startup, Reflection AI, claims it matches leading Chinese open-weight AI models with "3-4x less inference compute." That's it? Only 3 or 4 times? Wake me up when it's 10 times. At the end of the year, that could be year-end. Agents are all the rage, from Meta's Muse to xAI's Grokbot. They run on virtual machines in data centers but raise all sorts of privacy concerns. Startup Perplexity recently teamed up with Nvidia to run agents on PCs. Zero token costs. And you own your data. I often hear, that if tokens get cheaper, demand will go up. That's Jevens Paradox. Sure, elasticity works. But if prices drop 90%, demand must increase 900% just to stay flat. Remember when internet大厂 Meta's AI model on Global Crossing spectacularly failed because prices dropped too fast? Historically, semiconductors got 30% cheaper every year. When prices dropped by more than 50%, disaster struck with fabrication plant closings and company failures. Will 2026 be a data center? Again, timing is dicey. Current demand is gangbusters, but spending is a game of chicken until multiple factor-of-10 improvements kick in and prices collapse. This could set off a cascade of data-center halts and debt defaults, even as token demand increases. Yes, model training, drug discovery and winning prizes like the recently solved Navier-Stokes equations require hot chips in data centers. But chatbots and agents and other tasks may increasingly be handled on PCs and phones and smart glasses and whatever new gizmos Silicon Valley invents over the next decade. I've heard this called the "AI boom." The reason? The factor of 10 is visible now, as it often is, but ignored. Change doesn't happen overnight. It happens gradually, then suddenly. Write to kessler@wsi.com. # What Are U.S. Soldiers Doing in Ecuador? AMERICAS By Mary Anastasia O'Grady News that U.S. soldiers were deployed in Ecuador last month to fight drug-trafficking cartels deserves attention that it has received. A military officer pledge of President Trump is to stay out of "endless wars." Yet if ever there were a conflict destined to go on forever, it's the armed effort to defeat the suppliers of mind-altering substances in the face of robust consumer demand. This isn't to dismiss out of hand the shield of the American, the new U.S. regional security initiative under which the Ecuador mission was launched. The State Department says the goal of the hemispheric project, unveiled in March, is to pull together "likeminded allies" to "work together to advance strategies that stop foreign interference in our hemisphere, criminal and narco-terrorist gangs and cartels, and legal and mass immigration." Enhanced cooperation on the security interests of pro-Western countries in the hemispheric project is a welcome development. To the extent it's possible for the U.S. to assist neighbors in recovering democratic institutions that have been damaged by the war, the initiative has promise. But if the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition, operating under the "shield," requires sending American soldiers to fight in the jungles of far-flung lands, the risk of dangerous ground. The U.S. successfully supported Colombia and President Álvaro Uribe in that country's war against drug-trafficking rebels in the 2000s by helping with intelligence, equipment and training and by sending in a military. The U.S. has committed troops. A growing number of countries now welcome security help from the U.S. because armed groups have overwhelmed national police and military. The problems go well beyond narcotics production and trafficking. Criminal networks rule swaths of weak countries. They run extortion and kidnapping rackets, collect taxes, interfere with elections, traffic people, intimidate the political class with threats of violence, and run illegal gold-mining operations that trample the rights of mining companies. Quito is one of 19 governments that have joined the shield. Argentina, Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, Guatemala, Honduras, Peru and Panama are members. Four Caribbean countries, including the Dominican Republic, are in the group. Most member governments are center-right. Guatemala is one notable exception. All have reason to worry about threats to the United States' international criminal networks. Over the past decade drug traffickers searching for the path of least resistance from South America to the north have gravitated to Ecuador. The country has been republicated by political instability, its weak institutions, rampant corruption and attractive location made it a target for gangs looking to create a transit hub. It is now an organized-crime hot spot. ## Quito wants help in curbing cartel violence, but demand for drugs persists. As cartel violence has intensified and security has deteriorated, Ecuadorians have desperately sought a way back to the old tranquility they remember. President Daniel N. Booa won a special election in 2023 and a regular election in 2025 by promising to crack down on crime. But progress has been slow. The arrival of U.S. forces raised hopes that the tide will soon turn. In raids last month, Ecuadorian forces have killed 100 Americans, killed three alleged narcos and captured dozens more. Yet the broader strategy is to end the war in Ecuador. Colombia over the guerrillas and the paramilitary didn't end the flow of cocaine to the U.S. One reason is that America's demand for narcotics is inelastic: Even when the white hats reduce supply and prices go up, consumers keep buying. The net effect is that cartel in- come increases. Iliett groups aren't about to kill them. Their profitable businesses. But they can be cut down to size. The difficulty is finding a way to minimize their capacity to control territory without trampling civilian values. Mr. Uribe managed that. His government reestablished its authority across the country and restored it to its proper function of defending life and property without destroying democracy. Contrast that with El Salvador, which has gone the strongman route, employing high-powered weapons and sweeping lockups with no due process and at the expense of the country's economy. The U.S. has been exchanged for peace. Some political opponents of President Nayib Bukele have fled into exile. Sadly, the Trump administration celebrates Mr. Bukele. Ecuador could come out a winner if it can copy Colombia and avoid the error of El Salvador.
